games.title: Steroid and Sex Hormones: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the rate-limiting step in steroidogenesis?
questions.explanation: CYP11A1, also known as desmolase, catalyzes the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, which is the rate-limiting step in steroid hormone synthesis.

questions.q: A newborn presents with ambiguous genitalia, salt wasting, and hypotension. Laboratory tests show elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, leading to decreased cortisol and aldosterone, and shunting towards androgen production.

questions.q: Which circulating plasma protein binds testosterone and estradiol with the highest affinity?
questions.explanation: Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) binds sex steroids with high affinity, regulating their bioavailability in the circulation.

questions.q: In the peripheral tissues, testosterone is converted into its more potent derivative dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by which enzyme?
questions.explanation: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which has a significantly higher affinity for the androgen receptor.

questions.q: Which hormone exhibits a positive feedback mechanism on the hypothalamus and pituitary just prior to ovulation?
questions.explanation: A sustained high level of estradiol from the dominant follicle exerts a positive feedback effect on the hypothalamus and pituitary, triggering the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge.

questions.q: A patient with primary hypogonadism is expected to have which of the following hormone profiles?
options: Low testosterone, low LH, low FSH
Low testosterone, high LH, high FSH
High testosterone, low LH, low FSH
High testosterone, high LH, high FSH
questions.explanation: Primary hypogonadism involves testicular failure, which reduces negative feedback and leads to compensatory elevation of pituitary gonadotropins (LH and FSH).

questions.q: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of Cushing's syndrome due to an adrenal adenoma?
questions.explanation: An autonomous cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma suppresses pituitary ACTH release via negative feedback, resulting in low ACTH and high cortisol levels.

questions.q: During the normal menstrual cycle, which hormone predominates during the luteal phase?
questions.explanation: Progesterone is secreted in large amounts by the corpus luteum during the luteal phase to prepare the endometrium for potential implantation.

questions.q: Which of the following is synthesized primarily in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex due to the localized expression of aldosterone synthase?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) is uniquely expressed in the zona glomerulosa, enabling the synthesis of the mineralocorticoid aldosterone.

questions.q: Aromatase deficiency in a phenotypic female would most likely lead to which biochemical and clinical finding during puberty?
questions.explanation: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens; deficiency leads to androgen accumulation causing maternal virilization during pregnancy and primary amenorrhea with virilization in phenotypic females at puberty.

games.title: Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: Cases, Tumors, & Answers: quick quiz
games.topic: Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: Cases, Tumors, & Answers
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male presents with pain and swelling in his distal femur. Radiographs show a destructive lesion with a "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle. Biopsy reveals malignant osteoid production. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic radiographic features (sunburst, Codman's triangle) and histological finding of malignant osteoid production are characteristic of osteosarcoma.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, localized pain, and a rapidly growing mass in the diaphysis of the tibia. Radiographs show an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction. Histology reveals small, round, blue cells. Which genetic translocation is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.explanation: Ewing sarcoma, characterized by small round blue cells and an "onion-skin" appearance, is strongly associated with the t(11;22) translocation involving the EWSR1 and FLI1 genes.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female experiences knee pain. Imaging reveals an epiphyseal lesion of the distal femur that is lytic and extends to the articular surface. Histology shows numerous osteoclast-like giant cells uniformly distributed among mononuclear stromal cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Giant cell tumor of bone typically affects the epiphysis of long bones in young adults and is histologically characterized by abundant osteoclast-like giant cells within a background of mononuclear stromal cells.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, painful mass in his pelvis. Radiographs show a large, destructive lesion with mottled calcification. Biopsy reveals malignant cartilage production. Which of the following is the most common site for a primary chondrosarcoma?
questions.explanation: Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, particularly the pelvis, shoulder girdle, and ribs, in older adults.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous mass on their back that has been present for several years. Excisional biopsy shows mature adipocytes without atypia or mitotic activity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A lipoma is the most common benign soft tissue tumor, characterized by a well-circumscribed mass of mature adipocytes.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male develops a deep-seated mass near the knee. Histological examination reveals spindle cells arranged in fascicles and glandular structures. Immunohistochemistry is positive for cytokeratin and EMA. Which genetic alteration is characteristic of this tumor?
questions.explanation: Synovial sarcoma is characterized by the specific t(X;18) translocation, which fuses the SYT gene on chromosome 18 with one of the SSX genes on the X chromosome.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with a rapidly growing mass in the orbit. Biopsy reveals small, round, blue cells with occasional strap cells and cross-striations. Which subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma is most common in this age group and location?
questions.explanation: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common subtype in children and frequently arises in the head and neck region, including the orbit, and genitourinary tract.

questions.q: A young adult presents with a slowly progressive deformity of the femur. Radiographs show a "ground-glass" appearance with cortical thinning. Biopsy reveals curvilinear trabeculae of immature woven bone without osteoblastic rimming, set within a fibrous stroma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fibrous dysplasia is a developmental anomaly characterized by replacement of normal bone with immature woven bone in a fibrous stroma, often presenting with a "ground-glass" appearance on imaging.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most common malignant tumor found in bone?
questions.explanation: Metastatic tumors from other primary sites (e.g., breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) are far more common in bone than primary bone sarcomas.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy has a painless bony outgrowth near the knee joint. Radiographs show a bone spur with a cartilage cap, continuous with the underlying cortex and medullary cavity of the femur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An osteochondroma is the most common benign bone tumor, characterized by a cartilage-capped bony projection that arises from the external surface of a bone and is continuous with its cortex and medullary cavity.

games.title: Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 3-month history of dull, epigastric abdominal pain that occasionally wakes him at night and improves after meals. His mother notes a family history of peptic ulcer disease. Abdominal examination is unremarkable except for mild epigastric tenderness. What is the most definitive diagnostic test to confirm the underlying etiology?
options: Stool antigen test for Helicobacter pylori
Serum Helicobacter pylori IgG antibody testing
questions.explanation: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with antral biopsy for histology and culture is the gold standard diagnostic test for Helicobacter pylori infection in paediatric patients.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl with severe juvenile idiopathic arthritis presents to the emergency department with hematemesis and melena. She has been taking high-dose ibuprofen daily for the past 6 weeks without gastric protection. Vital signs show tachycardia and mild hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: High-dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use suppresses protective mucosal prostaglandins, making NSAID-induced peptic ulceration the most common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in this setting.

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl is diagnosed with Helicobacter pylori-associated duodenal ulcer disease via gastric biopsy during endoscopy. She has no known drug allergies and no prior exposure to macrolides. Which of the following is the recommended initial eradication regimen for this patient?
options: High-dose amoxicillin plus clarithromycin for 14 days
Proton pump inhibitor plus amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 14 days
Proton pump inhibitor plus metronidazole and doxycycline for 7 days
Proton pump inhibitor monotherapy for 8 weeks
questions.explanation: Standard first-line eradication therapy for paediatric Helicobacter pylori infection consists of a proton pump inhibitor combined with two antibiotics, typically amoxicillin and clarithromycin, for 14 days.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with a history of recurrent epigastric pain presents with sudden-onset, severe abdominal pain that began 2 hours ago. On examination, he is lying completely still with marked abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness, and absent bowel sounds. What is the next best diagnostic step?
options: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
questions.explanation: An upright chest radiograph is the initial diagnostic test of choice to rapidly identify pneumoperitoneum indicative of a perforated peptic ulcer.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy admitted to the paediatric intensive care unit following a severe 35% total body surface area thermal burn develops coffee-ground emesis on day 3 of admission. Laboratory testing reveals a acute drop in hemoglobin concentration. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying this patient's condition?
options: Gastric mucosal ischemia secondary to systemic hypoperfusion
Direct mucosal injury from bacterial translocation
Hypergastrinemia secondary to a neuroendocrine tumor
Increased intracranial pressure leading to vagal stimulation
questions.explanation: Stress-induced mucosal lesions (Curling ulcers) in severe burn patients result primarily from gastric mucosal ischemia secondary to systemic hypoperfusion and splanchnic vasoconstriction.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with recurrent, refractory peptic ulcer disease and chronic watery diarrhea. Endoscopy reveals multiple ulcers in the distal duodenum and jejunum that have failed to heal despite high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy. Which diagnostic laboratory test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A markedly elevated fasting serum gastrin level is the initial diagnostic test of choice to evaluate for a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) in a patient with refractory, atypical peptic ulcers.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with peripheral edema, lethargy, and recurrent postprandial vomiting over the past 2 weeks. Laboratory workup reveals profound hypoalbuminemia (1.8 g/dL) without proteinuria, and endoscopy demonstrates giant hypertrophic gastric folds with excessive mucus production. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Paediatric Menetrier disease is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy often triggered by CMV infection, characterized by giant gastric mucosal folds, hypersecretion of mucus, and protein-losing enteropathy.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy with a 6-month history of unmanaged epigastric pain presents with persistent non-bilious vomiting occurring 1 to 2 hours after meals. Physical examination reveals visible upper abdominal distension and a succussion splash on abdominal auscultation. What is the most likely complication of his condition?
questions.explanation: Chronic peptic ulceration near the pyloric channel can cause edema and scarring, leading to gastric outlet obstruction characterized by postprandial non-bilious vomiting and a succussion splash.

games.title: Paed 2021: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 4-month-old male infant presents with a 2-day history of low-grade fever, coryza, and cough. On examination, he has tachypnoea, subcostal retractions, diffuse expiratory wheezing, and fine crackles throughout both lung fields. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute bronchiolitis typically affects infants under 1 year of age and presents with coryza, cough, tachypnoea, subcostal retractions, and widespread crackles or wheezes.

questions.q: A 7-month-old female infant is brought to the emergency department with episodic, severe abdominal pain during which she draws her knees to her chest, followed by lethargy. Examination reveals a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant and 'red currant jelly' stool on rectal exam. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic intervention?
questions.explanation: An air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic for intussusception in hemodynamically stable infants.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 6-day history of high persistent fever, non-purulent bilateral conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, and a strawberry tongue. Examination also demonstrates a polymorphous trunk rash and desquamation of the skin on his fingertips. What is the most appropriate immediate management to prevent coronary artery complications?
questions.explanation: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) combined with aspirin within 10 days of fever onset significantly reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysm formation in Kawasaki disease.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic due to worsening periorbital swelling in the mornings and abdominal distension over the past week. Urinalysis demonstrates 4+ proteinuria with no hematuria, and blood tests show a serum albumin of 18 g/L with normal renal function. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children, presenting with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and generalized edema without hematuria.

questions.q: An 18-month-old male infant presents late at night with a 1-day history of low-grade fever, a harsh 'barking' cough, and inspiratory stridor at rest. Physical examination reveals mild intercostal recessions and an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: A single dose of oral dexamethasone is recommended for all children with croup to reduce upper airway inflammation.

questions.q: An 8-year-old girl presents with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss, now presenting with lethargy and deep, rapid (Kussmaul) respirations. Venous blood gas reveals a pH of 7.12, serum bicarbonate of 10 mmol/L, and a blood glucose level of 24 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy following fluid resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Following initial fluid resuscitation, a continuous intravenous soluble insulin infusion is the mainstay of treatment for paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.q: A 4-week-old first-born male infant presents with a 5-day history of worsening non-bilious, projectile vomiting immediately after feeds. On physical examination, he shows signs of dehydration and a small, firm, olive-sized mass is palpable in the epigastrium. What venous blood gas abnormality is most characteristic of this condition?
questions.explanation: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes persistent loss of gastric hydrochloric acid from vomiting, leading to a classic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.q: A 2-year-old unimmunized girl presents with a 4-day history of high fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Examination reveals tiny white lesions on an erythematous base on her buccal mucosa, alongside a maculopapular rash spreading downward from her face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa combined with the prodromal triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by a descending maculopapular rash are pathognomonic for measles.

games.title: Human Pathology — Course Outline: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following classes of anti-inflammatory drugs acts primarily by inhibiting the enzyme cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis?
questions.explanation: COX-2 selective inhibitors belong to the NSAID class and decrease inflammation by blocking prostaglandin production.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of low-dose aspirin in the prevention of myocardial infarction and stroke?
options: Reversible blockade of P2Y12 ADP receptors
questions.explanation: Low-dose aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, preventing the formation of thromboxane A2 and subsequent platelet aggregation.

questions.q: Which characteristic side effect is most classically associated with chronic, high-dose corticosteroid therapy such as prednisone?
questions.explanation: Chronic systemic corticosteroid use mimics Cushing syndrome and commonly induces bone mineral loss leading to osteoporosis.

questions.q: What is the primary clinical indication for methotrexate when used in chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis?
options: As an immunosuppressant and anti-inflammatory agent
As an acute rescue medication for gouty arthritis
As a direct-acting thrombolytic for deep vein thrombosis
As an antibiotic for septic arthritis
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is widely used as a first-line DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis due to its potent immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory properties.

questions.q: Which of the following medications is classified as a biologic TNF-alpha inhibitor used in the treatment of autoimmune inflammatory diseases like Crohn disease and rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody that neutralizes TNF-alpha, dampening the chronic inflammatory cascade in autoimmune diseases.

questions.q: What is the main mechanism of action of allopurinol in the long-term management of gout?
options: Inhibition of xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid production
Increasing renal excretion of uric acid in the proximal tubules
Direct enzymatic degradation of uric acid to allantoin
Reduction of neutrophil migration into the joint space
questions.explanation: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that blocks the biochemical pathway leading to uric acid synthesis.

questions.q: Which of the following adverse effects is classically associated with the use of acetaminophen (paracetamol) in massive overdosage?
questions.explanation: Acetaminophen overdose leads to the accumulation of a toxic metabolite (NAPQI) that causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of unfractionated heparin in anticoagulation?
options: Potentiation of antithrombin III activity to inhibit thrombin and factor Xa
Direct inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase
Binding directly to the active site of circulating thrombin
Inhibition of vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis
questions.explanation: Heparin binds to antithrombin III, drastically accelerating its ability to neutralize thrombin and factor Xa.

games.title: Male reproductive system — Past Paper: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is prescribed finasteride to reduce prostate size. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
questions.explanation: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase, preventing the peripheral conversion of testosterone to its more potent form, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), thereby reducing prostate volume.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man is started on tamsulosin for lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia. What is the primary mechanism by which tamsulosin improves urinary airflow?
options: Selective blockade of alpha-1A adrenergic receptors in the prostate
Competitive inhibition of 5-alpha reductase in stromal tissue
Direct activation of beta-3 adrenergic receptors in the detrusor muscle
Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase-2 in prostatic epithelium
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin selectively blocks alpha-1A adrenergic receptors in the prostate and bladder neck, causing smooth muscle relaxation and rapid relief of urinary outflow obstruction.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man who takes isosorbide mononitrate for stable angina requests a prescription for sildenafil to treat erectile dysfunction. Why is the combination of these two drugs strictly contraindicated?
options: Risk of severe hypertension from excessive release of endothelin-1
Increased risk of ischemic stroke via drug-induced platelet aggregation
Profound hypotension due to synergistic accumulation of intracellular cGMP
Acute kidney injury secondary to skeletal muscle rhabdomyolysis
questions.explanation: Combining phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitors like sildenafil with nitrates causes massive, uncontrolled accumulation of cGMP, leading to life-threatening hypotension.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is initiated on the GnRH agonist leuprorelin. Why is an androgen receptor antagonist (such as bicalutamide) co-administered during the first few weeks of therapy?
options: To prevent severe hyperkalemia caused by mineralocorticoid excess
To treat co-existing lower urinary tract symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia
To decrease the rapid hepatic metabolism and clearance of leuprorelin
To prevent a transient testosterone surge and initial tumor flare
questions.explanation: GnRH agonists initially stimulate pituitary receptors, causing a temporary flare in LH and testosterone levels that can worsen tumor symptoms unless blocked by an anti-androgen.

questions.q: A 74-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer is started on abiraterone acetate. Which enzyme does this drug selectively inhibit to block adrenal and intratumoral androgen biosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Abiraterone acetate inhibits CYP17, a crucial enzyme in the androgen synthesis pathway within testicular, adrenal, and prostatic neoplasm tissues.

questions.q: Which of the following medications acts as a non-steroidal competitive antagonist at androgen receptors and is frequently used in the management of prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: Bicalutamide is a non-steroidal anti-androgen that competitively inhibits the binding of dihydrotestosterone and testosterone to androgen receptors in target tissues.

questions.q: A patient with erectile dysfunction who is unresponsive to oral PDE-5 inhibitors is prescribed intracavernosal injections of alprostadil. What is the mechanism of action of alprostadil?
options: Nitric oxide donor that directly activates soluble guanylyl cyclase
Synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue that increases intracellular cAMP
Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist causing vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Alprostadil is a synthetic analogue of prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) that stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP levels to relax cavernosal smooth muscle.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man with advanced prostate cancer requires immediate androgen deprivation therapy without experiencing an initial hormone flare. Which of the following drugs acts as a GnRH receptor antagonist to achieve immediate testosterone suppression?
questions.explanation: Degarelix is a GnRH antagonist that directly and competitively blocks pituitary GnRH receptors, causing rapid suppression of LH and testosterone without an initial hormonal surge.
